chunks: Meaning of "general purpose" in GPIO. The question: What does "GP" refer to?
"General purpose" means a pin is not tied to one fixed job. A general-purpose pin has no assigned job until software gives it one.
Software picks whether it is an input or an output, and what level it drives. In practice these pins are shared with other functions, and they are not all identical.
Picture a hotel with a few fixed-use rooms, such as the ice machine room and the lobby, which can never be anything else.
The rest are general rooms that can be booked as a bedroom or a meeting room. A booking board decides each room's use at any moment.
But the rooms differ: some have a window, some are wheelchair-accessible. The booking board is the pin multiplexer, and the room features are things like 5 volts tolerance.
One physical pad, several possible owners. The mux selects exactly one at a time.
Plain "GPIO" is just one of the choices, which is why the pin is called general-purpose: its default owner is the software-visible port.
Dedicated pin: a pin with one fixed job, such as power, ground, reset or the clock crystal. General-purpose pin: a pin whose role is chosen in software.
Pin multiplexing (alternate function): a selector in front of the pin that connects it to the plain GPIO block or to a built-in hardware block (a peripheral), such as a serial port's transmit line.
High-impedance input: the usual state right after reset. The pin neither drives nor loads the wire. 5 volts tolerant: able to accept 5 volts on a 3. 3 volts chip.
Say a 48-pin microcontroller uses 9 pins for power, ground, reset, crystal and dedicated USB. That leaves at most 48 minus 9 equals 39 general-purpose pins.
If your design needs a UART (2 pins), SPI (4 pins) and I2C (2 pins), those peripherals take 8 of them, and 31 remain for plain GPIO.
Also, after reset those pins float as inputs, so any external part wired to them must be safe in that state. That is the whole idea.
"GP means general-purpose: the pin has no fixed job, so software decides whether it's an input or an output and what level it drives.
That contrasts with dedicated pins like power, ground, reset or the crystal, which always do one thing.
In practice GPIO pins are multiplexed with peripherals, so the same pad can be a GPIO, a UART TX, a PWM output or an ADC input depending on configuration.
And general doesn't mean identical: some pins are 5 volts tolerant, analog capable or boot straps, so I check the datasheet's pin table when assigning."
